utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This morning, Mr. Lukic, I think, because Mr. Krgovic had indicated that you had a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Mr. Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you questions on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic. More specifically, what I want to know is about the exchanges, and I will ask you right away, Mr. Simeunovic: In your work - and I'm interested in the period of 1992 and 1993 - did you work on the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the period of 1992. Even nowadays I'm still a member of the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First let me ask you: When did you start working on these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working on the exchanges, so to speak, from the very beginning, immediately after hostilities broke out in the general area of northeast Bosnia, in May. There were prisoners on both sides already, so it was necessary to start work on the exchanges, and I was involved right from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which commission did you take part in? What was its name and what was your position in it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for military commissions for the exchange of prisoners of war and deceased persons. At first they were at brigade levels, but after that, a corps commission for the exchange was established, and I immediately became a member of the corps commission of the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly when you became a member of the commission of the East Bosnian Corps? Do you remember the month, or at least the season, when this began?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was towards the end of June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many members did this commission have during your work? I'm referring to the commission of the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had five members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your role in that commission? Did you have any particular position or were you merely a member?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the whole of this time I was a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other members, were they also military officers, or were there civilians there too?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to this commission of which you were a member, will you please tell us whether there were any other military commissions, and I'm referring to the army of Republika Srpska, and with what other commissions did you cooperate?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In each corps of the army of Republika Srpska there was a military commission. In my work, I cooperated a lot with the commission from the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember the president of that commission in the period that we are interested in, 1992 and 1993? What was the person's name?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Grujicic. He was the president of this commission of the 1st Krajina Corps in the period between 1992 and 1993. That was him. He was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a state commission at that time, and where was it based? Can you perhaps tell us?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a state commission at that time, and its headquarters was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it too have military officers as members?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, most of them were civilians. There were no military officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that those were people from the Ministry of Justice? Please tell us if you know.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the members were people from the Ministry of Justice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us now: In your work on these exchanges, did you cooperate with civilian commissions too?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. In our work, we cooperated with civilian commissions. We had to cooperate with them, for the simple reason that municipal civilian commissions were not able to carry out an exchange at the separation line without military commissions. There had to be a ceasefire first established by someone for the exchange to take place. That was what the cooperation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us with which specific municipal commissions you cooperated, in view of the area of responsibility of the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cooperated with the Bijeljina municipal commission, with the Brcko municipal commission, with the Samac municipal commission, the Modrica municipal commission, the Doboj municipal commission, the Vlasenica municipal commission. Wherever there was a municipal commission covering the area of responsibility of the East Bosnian Corps or the 1st Krajina Corps, I worked with those commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received a remark from our case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 4, line 8, you said that as a military structure you had to secure a ceasefire and that that was why there was cooperation between the civilian and military commissions. It was through the military structures that a ceasefire was brokered?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only way to arrange for a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So civilian commissions would go to you and speak to you about that, you as the military commissions. Would they simply join you once you had brokered those ceasefires? What was the procedure like? Could civilian commissions just simply go on their own to the separation lines where exchanges were carried out or were they always accompanied by military commissions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian commissions could not go on their own to the separation lines between the warring factions. They always went when a military commission went, when there was an exchange to be carried out. They would join and bring up their own subjects at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With which commissions of the opposing sides, let me say, did you negotiate? Can you please just try to enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We negotiated with the Tuzla commission, which was also a military commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In whose hands was Tuzla at that time? Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tuzla was under the area of responsibility of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. We also cooperated with commissions under the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, in Posavina, and we also cooperated with a commission from the Republic of Croatia. We cooperated with other commissions too from the canton Zenica, Bihac and so on and so forth. We did have cooperation with most of the commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've outlined the general framework of your activity, I would like to ask you the following: What was the main goal and task of your work on these exchanges, you as a commission? What did you usually discuss and what decisions did you take?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understood you correctly. You want me to explain the method of our work?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what or who you discussed or talked about, and then please explain what the procedure or method of your work was, the work of your commission.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a military commission, we spoke about prisoners of war who were military officers. We spoke about those who had been killed or those who had gone missing. We spoke on behalf of Republika Srpska and they spoke on behalf of their own side, their own persons, whether the BH army or the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the procedure like? Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber briefly? What was the subject of those negotiations and what would you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would meet the opposing side, and at this meeting we would exchange lists of persons. We gave them our own list of persons we were looking for and they would give us theirs, following which we would verify the whereabouts of persons that they were looking for, in which military prisons those persons were incarcerated. We would check whether they were somewhere in our area of responsibility or whether those persons were actually in areas of responsibility covered by a different corps. Once we managed to track down these persons, we would draw up a list of persons found within our area of responsibility or persons we managed to locate within someone else's area of responsibility, and then this list would be forwarded to the security organ of the corps in our own area of responsibility or someone else's area of responsibility, again if such persons were found in someone else's area of responsibility. After that, the security organs would provide specific individual explanations pertaining to each person, whether a person could be exchanged or not. Once we had that, we have a complete list and go back to negotiating with the other side. We give them a list of persons that we've managed to track down and who could be exchanged. After that, we would have another request in case there were no changes or additions by the other side, and this request would again be forwarded to the security organ, and the security organ would give approval for the persons from the list to be exchanged. And then the place and time would be determined for the exchange, and the exchange would be carried out. If a person happened to be on one of these lists against whom criminal proceedings were under way, or a person who has already been convicted, we were not allowed to exchange these persons. For that, we had to receive approval from the security organs of the General Staff. They were the only ones who could give approval for such persons to be or not to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you need to have approval from the military prosecutor or military courts? In which period exactly and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was necessary too. The security organ, once we have forwarded the list of persons we were looking for, they would go to military courts and military prosecutors to verify whether there were criminal proceedings under way against any of the persons, and on the basis of that, we would receive feedback from them with the list of persons who could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. I wonder whether, Mr. Simeunovic, you would know: What type of criminal proceedings are we talking about? Are we talking about criminal proceedings for ordinary crimes and the domestic law in Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina, or are we talking about criminal proceedings for, shall we say, violations of military law or for violations of the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions? What type of criminal proceedings are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to our rules, and pursuant to our instructions, persons who had been convicted for war crimes could not be exchanged. Those persons were simply not exchanged, persons convicted of war crimes or crimes against humanity. That would have barred them from being exchanged. However, persons who had convictions for illegal armament, or joining forces against the army of Republika Srpska, there were criminal proceedings under way against such persons or such persons were convicted, but those people in theory could have been exchanged, it's just that it took approval from higher military organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just prepared some documents now that will point this out even more clearly, Your Honour Judge Williams. I would like PDB 92/3 [Realtime transcript read in error "96/2"] to be shown now, please. I said 92. I said 92, but the transcript says 96. However, I see that the witness has the right document in front of him nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, I believe that you are quite familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are rules for the work of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war in the zone of responsibility of the East Bosnian Corps, and I am quite familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to look at a few articles, and I would like to hear your comments on that. However, my first question relates to the date. I see that the date is the 7th of March, 1993. Did you work according to these rules before that date, and which documents did you base your work upon before you adopted these rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the commission, the military commission of the East Bosnian Corps, had been established sometime in June 1992. At that time, until these rules entered into force, we worked according to instructions given by the East Bosnian Corps and by the orders issued by the command. Later on they were simply transformed into these rules and regulations. So we actually worked the same way before. We worked when the rules came into force the same way we did before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into detail, because I think that you have quite literally explained everything that is written here, notably, articles 9, 10, and 11. But could you please take a look and could you -- could you please have a look at articles 9, 10, and 11, and is that the procedure that you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We worked in accordance with these rules and that is the procedure that I explained a short while ago. We worked according to these rules. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at Article 13. Tell me: Was this the principle that governed the exchanges? Were the exchanges conducted on a one-for-one basis, one soldier for one soldier, et cetera? What about officers? Was there a single principle involved for all commissions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the principle of exchange: One-for-one, one officer for one officer. We abided by those rules. There is also the principle of all-for-all. We tried to carry that through, but we never managed to organise that kind of an exchange, one that was based on the principle of all-for-all. But we did abide by the one-for-one principle, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at Article 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Before you move to 16, I see that Mr. Simeunovic, the underlining was put in by hand on the B/C/S text, and I refer to that simply because, of course, in the English text it's printed underlining. And Article 13, in the English text, not only talks about the one-for-one basis of soldier for soldier, it also goes on then to say: Woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person. Now, I thought Article 13 and this document is referring to the exchange of prisoners of war. So may I ask you: Why is there reference not only soldier for soldier, which of course could be male or female, but then also specifically woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person? How come they were being classified as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it says here, because women were also participants as military conscripts. They also took part in war operations. Perhaps not in the first line of combat, but they did participate in both warring parties. Also there were elderly people. There were volunteers who, according to our rules, could not have been included in military units, but they were there as volunteers, let's put it that way. They wanted to take part. This is what the rules say, but I do not remember that I ever had a single woman involved in any exchange. There were women who were killed, but there weren't any women that were exchanged that I can remember. There were some elderly persons, though, who were exchanged just like soldiers were, but there weren't any women. That's why the rules included this. In the commissions, all involved were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the use, to your knowledge, of the word "soldier" was exclusively with reference to male soldiers, based on what you've just said. Because you're saying women could be conscripts, and so on and so forth, so your reference here to soldier is exclusively, if I understand you correctly, referring to those of the male gender.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm referring to women soldiers as well. I said that in our army, the army of Republika Srpska, there were women who were soldiers too. Also on the other sides, in the other warring parties, there were women soldiers as well. There were also elderly people. Most of them were men, the elderly people. According to the criteria that were in force, they did not have military obligation to report to a military unit, but they came on a voluntary basis. They volunteered. That is why it says specifically "women" and all the rest. But we considered all prisoners of war as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, let's just have Article 16 explained as well. As for Article 16, I'm interested in the following: There is something that is written here, and you'll tell me whether this is the way it was in practice, namely, the written opinion of the security organ. For every exchange that you worked on, was it indispensable to have the opinion of the security organ presented in writing, as it is put here, and was this really applied in practice? That is what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is the way it was in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see a suggestion coming from my client now in relation to the explanations you gave a few minutes ago related to all-for-all exchanges. Do you remember the exchange in Sibosnica? At that time, was an attempt made to carry out an all-for-all exchange?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 21st of July, 1993. The exchange in Sibosnica, at the separation line, the line that separated the warring parties. We tried to carry out this exchange on an all-for-all basis; however, later we came to realise that it was not an all-for-all exchange. There were some people who stayed behind in prisons in Tuzla, so they came only subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber why was this agreement not honoured, the one that was based on an all-for-all principle.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it wasn't honoured, but this agreement was not honoured because the opposing side did not bring in all the prisoners of war who were in prison in Tuzla at that moment. Later on, they tried to justify this by saying that these people had been incarcerated in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like us to get a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is D166/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you said a while ago, that civilian exchanges were linked to what you did, because only when you organised exchanges could they do anything, tell me: Was there any other form of cooperation between military and civilian commissions? Was there exchange of information about prisoners? And what was this relationship like between civilian and military commissions, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, cooperation did not only mean that we should make it possible for them to come to the separation line and to carry out the exchange. With all commissions, we also exchanged opinions. We looked for people that they were looking for. We tried to find out more about them. There were commissions from a wider territory, one that went beyond the area of responsibility of the East Bosnian Corps. So we certainly asked these commissions for information too. However, as the military commission, we did not decide --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to deal with this separately. We're going to deal with this separately. Tell me: Was there a practice or a tendency for families to go at the same time, or rather, to have family reunification, if that is what people wanted? Was there cooperation in that sense between military and civilian commissions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was cooperation. If it was not possible to organise an exchange the same day, both of civilian prisoners and of prisoners of war, then if a group of prisoners of war would leave, then at the very next agreement with the other side, the state commission would be present - I mean the civilian commission - and they brought civilian persons who wanted to follow their men, I mean their husbands, brothers, who had gone to the other side, who had been exchanged previously as prisoners of war. Sometimes it wasn't possible to organise both at the same time, but there were such cases that there were even simultaneous exchanges of prisoners of war and of civilians who wanted to cross over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you the following. When I asked you to pause a minute ago, because this is something that we clearly have to distinguish. In their work, did military commissions interfere in the decision-making of civilian commissions or the negotiations that were organised by civilian commissions?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have the right to interfere with the negotiations of civilian commissions. Also we did not allow civilian commissions to interfere in our negotiations, in our work, in the work of the military commission alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could any member of the civilian commission ask or insist or give its consent for a person who had the status of a military prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the civilian commission could ask but could not give consent. They could ask through the military commissions. Perhaps they were under pressure of family members or whatever. Perhaps they could ask whether the family could be prepared to cross over at the same time. But a member of the civilian commission could not decide about a prisoner of war going to be exchanged. That is a decision that could only be passed by military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Simeunovic -- or let me ask you something else. Concerning your work on exchanges, did you cooperate with Mr. Miroslav Tadic, one of the accused persons here?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did cooperate with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember when you started contacts related to exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Tadic, did you also cooperate with Mr. Veljo Maslic from Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was the president of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you cooperate with them along the same lines as with the other civilian commissions that you have talked about?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had the same kind of cooperation along the same lines and principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Could I just get some clarification? He indicated that he cooperated with Miroslav Tadic at the end of 1992. Is that the same time period, or could we have some time period that this witness cooperated with Mr. Veljo Maslic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard the question. When you talked about starting to cooperate with Mr. Tadic towards the end of 1992, does the same apply to Mr. Maslic, or no?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the same applies to Mr. Maslic. At that point he was already president of that civilian commission, as far as I know. That was the period of my cooperation with them, since the end of 1992, and we continued to cooperate as long as there was any need for the work of these commissions to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned during the examination-in-chief the other day when the army of Republika Srpska was restructured and reorganised, that Mr. Beronja appointed Mr. Jez head of security, as far as I understood, Captain Jez, and that in that period you remained in your position as a security officer, as far as I remember. There is one thing I would like to know in connection with Mr. Jez: What was his relationship with Mr. Stevan Todorovic and the Special Forces of volunteers from Serbia? Do you know that? On what sort of terms were they, as you had similar positions, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Major Mile Beronja was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, he appointed Captain Jez as a security officer, and he appointed me as intelligence officer. I told you that these two positions were separated. He had, in fact, separated them. The cooperation of Captain Jez, because I didn't even know his first name at that time, his cooperation with Stevan Todorovic and the Special Forces that were there was close. I remember that we carried out arrests. When I say "we," I mean the army of Republika Srpska. We carried out an arrest of Captain Jez. That was in Donji Zabar. That was a forward command post of the East Bosnian Corps. He was arrested because of their [as interpreted] cooperation with them and because of certain criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on to another subject which is also related to exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one word here on page 17, line 4. He was arrested because of "his" instead of "their." It should read "his cooperation with them," meaning Captain Jez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to ask you several questions about Batkovic. We can use the term "collection centre" or "Detention Centre." My colleagues from the Prosecution used the term "camp." But what I want to know is when the Batkovic centre was established. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collection centre at Batkovic was established after the collection centre at Manjaca was closed down. That's also when the collection centre at Bijeljina, that is, in Batkovic, which is a village close to Bijeljina, was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please determine the time period? Was that in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1993. I don't think I can remember the exact date, but I think it was perhaps towards the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have information that the prisoners from Samac were transferred to Batkovic towards the end of 1992, so it may as well have been the end of 1992. Who established this collection centre and who controlled it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collection centre at Batkovic was under the East Bosnian Corps command. This means that it was also established by the East Bosnian Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The warden of this prison, was he a military officer? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Djoko Pajic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Djoko Pajic was the head of the collection centre at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit D40/ID. May I please add: D40/3 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the signature on page 2. Are you familiar with that signature, and tell me that first, please. Is this the man I have asked you about?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commander of the collection centre, Major Djoko Pajic. That's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information that judicial organs visited the collection centre and requested data, as it reads in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... On the ELMO B/C/S version instead of English version, because our clients do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, they can have the B/C/S version on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that judicial organs came to the collection centre, and they simply requested information regarding persons who were being detained there. They wanted to know whether there were criminal proceedings against any of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to now please tender this into evidence, because this was only for identification when Witness Mehinovic was here. We mistakenly gave him page 1 only and then additionally we found page 2. And my friends from the Prosecution asked that this not be given a full evidence number. But since our witness today has just identified the person who signed this document, I think there is no longer anything to dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a number, please, or can we confirm that it will retain the same number as an exhibit this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D40/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, who could have entered the prison in Batkovic, and who was in charge of giving approval for someone to enter the prison in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Permission to enter the collection centre in Batkovic was given by the security organ of the East Bosnian Corps, and you needed to have this permission to enter the collection centre. That was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of civilian commissions also went into Batkovic and took prisoners out to be exchanged? If so, tell us, please, what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. A person who was a member of a civilian commission could also enter the collection centre in Batkovic. They would have a list, a previously drafted list, and they would take prisoners away with them. But they needed to be granted approval by a military commission from a corps. As long as it was outside the area of the East Bosnian Corps, then this person had to have permission to be able to enter the collection centre at Batkovic, collect the persons included on the list and take them to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said according to a list that had been delivered previously. Does that mean that the prison command would be given a list, regardless of whether a civilian, a member of a civilian commission or a member of a military commission would be there to collect it, and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I explained about the working method of the commissions for the exchange of prisoners, once there was a final list of persons who could be exchanged, the same list would be forwarded to the commander of the collection centre at Batkovic, and then two or three days before the scheduled exchange, they would make sure that those persons included on the list were there at the collection centre on that day. Some persons were listed as being in the collection centre, but perhaps these persons were at a certain point in time elsewhere, going after different duties. So two or three days ahead of a scheduled exchange, the list of persons to be exchanged would be forwarded to the head or commander of the collection centre, and only those persons whose names were included on the list could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would have been my next question. Was it possible at all for a person who was not on the list to be taken away for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't possible. The list would be forwarded to the commander of the collection centre two or three days before the actual collection and exchange, and only those persons who were on the list could be exchanged. You couldn't change any of the names on the day of the exchange and replace it with a different name. No one could change the decision handed down by the security organ, by the corps security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to those lists of exchanged persons after the exchange? Were they registered and recorded?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon completion of an exchange, the president of the commission was duty-bound to draw up a report on the exchange, including the persons who were exchanged and the persons who arrived for an exchange, and then this report would be forwarded to the security organ of the corps. Persons who left the collection centre to go to an exchange, their names would be entered into a computerised database at the security organ, and they always had this information ready for retrieval. So it wasn't possible for a person who was listed to be exchanged to go or to be replaced by someone who was not on any of the lists of persons to be exchanged. At least as long as I was there, this never occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show the witness document internal number PDB 101/3. Not this one; the other one. Yes. Not the one you have in front of you. This will not be needed right now. Can you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you read this? Can you please tell us: Was there a court and a prosecutor with the East Bosnian Corps, and where was the Court of the prosecutor based?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the military prosecutor at the East Bosnian Corps command, based in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document speaks for itself, but even so, could you please explain the first passage, line 3. It says: "From the administration of the OB affairs." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: OB means security and intelligence affairs. That's what the abbreviation stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please read out, slowly, the first sentence of the second passage, the first two lines. Because the translation is inaccurate, and I think the whole thing is perfectly legible, especially the word that the translators claim they couldn't read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could you just please read out slowly the first two lines of the second passage.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Namely, such approval is granted according to instructions by the judicial organs of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the rest is perfectly legible. It was about the word "judicial." Was this regular procedure for the prosecutor, when addressed by a security organ, to issue such an opinion?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a matter of regular procedure in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a number for this document to be tendered into evidence, if there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see none. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D167/3, and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have merely a couple of questions left. Mr. Simeunovic, can you please tell us, according to your information: Why did representatives of civilian commissions go to take prisoners away? Why was this the case, if we know that there were military commissions who were in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that if the exchange was organised by the 1st Krajina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska, and the prisons to be collected were at the Batkovic collection centre, so as to avoid a member of a commission coming all the way from Banja Luka to Batkovic. Then they would simply grant their approval, their consent, for a civilian official, a member of a civilian commission in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, to collect the prisoners and to bring them to the determined place of exchange. But this approval was given for merely technical reason. As concerns the East Bosnian Corps, no persons ever went there, simply because the seat -- its seat was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have information that civilians also left often during these exchanges, or when prisoners were taken over, in order to be taken to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said: Whenever this was technically feasible, exchanges were organised of prisoners of war, and their families, if they chose to do so, would go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one more document which I would like to have shown to the witness, the one that was internally marked PDB 129/3. It's already in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this document familiar to you, or is this type of document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is familiar to me. We, as a commission, had it. But there were many other such documents that we received from the collection centre in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all persons who were in Batkovic have this same status of war prisoners, prisoners of war? You see, it says so down here.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had the status of prisoners of war. All persons who were at the collection centre in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here - and it will be of interest to the Trial Chamber - the names of a few persons who appeared in these proceedings. This involves quite a few different localities. But do you know from where, from which territory, persons were taken from to Batkovic? Was it only within your area of responsibility or did it come from other areas as well, if I can put it this way?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were persons there who had come from the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not only persons who were in the area of responsibility of the East Bosnian Corps. When the collection centre at Manjaca was abolished, persons from that centre were transferred to the Batkovic centre too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to get a number for this document as well, if the Prosecution doesn't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection. Could we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D168/3, and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, I'm about to finish my questions. The last question I have for you, which is based on your first answer: You said that until the present day, you work at the commission. You said that it is today called the state commission for seeking missing persons. Since you worked with Tadic, do you know whether Tadic, until his voluntary surrender to this Tribunal, cooperated with this commission, and did he offer his help in this regard? Did you talk to him in relation to this work pertaining to the quest for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Dayton Agreement had already been signed, Tadic was not a collaborator of the state commission, but he continued offering his help, and we, if necessary, took some information from him, or whatever else was needed. Because for many years he had worked in the commission for exchanges. Not only from him, but also from all members of the commission, we seek information, and people are glad to give such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simeunovic. My name is Phillip Weiner and I'm going to be asking you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified on Thursday - I'm sorry - on Wednesday, February 26th, about the arrival of some Serbian volunteers. You said they arrived at Batkusa in JNA helicopters. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said that Stevan Todorovic and the commander of the 1st Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group were there.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic and the commander of the 1st Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, Mico Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were both present?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that time you met three of the leaders, or the three leaders of the volunteers, or paramilitaries, whatever you want to call them: Crni, Debeli, and Lugar?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not meet them. I just saw them come there. Later on I found out what their names were, but at that moment, when they arrived, I did not even know who they were. I had just assumed because they came and said hello to Stevan Todorovic, that they were the leaders of the group that had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, are you aware that Simo Zaric has provided three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, he's been interviewed and given three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but it is quite natural that he should be giving statements to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on, the one facing the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure the usher can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in Simo Zaric's third statement, which is Exhibit P142 ter, Simo Zaric discusses the arrival of this Serbian volunteers, as you did, and he indicates that Stevan Todorovic and Dr. Blagoje Simic were involved in bringing them to Samac. On page 73, Zaric is asked about the names of the Serbian paramilitaries who came to town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could the witness be shown this document P142 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you could please turn to page 74, please. If you could go to the top paragraph on page 74, the second sentence up from the bottom. So let me bring you back. The second sentence from the bottom of that top paragraph. Do you see? He's asked on the page before about the names of the Serbian paramilitaries who came to town, and as he describes that, he also says: "Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Simic certainly knew, with certain forces in Serbia that they had contacts with, that they agreed with about the group that was supposed to arrive." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Stevan Todorovic met this group. At that time, Blagoje Simic was not in the village of Batkusa when these people arrived. Perhaps Simo could have obtained some other information in Belgrade or something, but I know that it was Stevan Todorovic who met them, and the commander of the 1st Detachment too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What it was is Simo Zaric is commenting that those two persons were involved in bringing them to Samac, that they knew about their arrival coming -- was forthcoming. And did I read that correctly: When Simo Zaric in explaining that, says: "Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Simic certainly knew, with certain forces in Serbia that they had contacts with, that they agreed with about the group that was supposed to arrive"? Isn't that what happened in Samac: Those persons - Blagoje Simic and Todorovic - were aware that those persons were arriving and were involved or participated in bringing them there, based on your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have knowledge that Stevan Todorovic knew about this because he's the one who met them. Now, whether Blagoje Simic knew about it is something that I did not know about at that time. I know that Blagoje Simic was president of the Crisis Staff. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Weiner. Just for the sake of clarity of the transcript. If you take a look at your question on page 19, beginning, I think, line 17 on the LiveNote, there are all sorts of things left out of what you said, and for the sake of us coming back and reading that a bit later on, it doesn't make too much sense. Do you see what I'm referring to? Your question, it's gone off the big screen here, but on page 27, line 17, where you asked the witness to turn to page 74, and then three lines down you say the second sentence, et cetera. "Do you see." And then what you say hasn't come out clearly at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll continue on with that question and comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric made an indication in 1998 that those persons were aware and planned with people in Belgrade for the paramilitaries to come there. You stated, just previously, that you didn't know at that time, upon the arrival. Did you sometime later learn that Blagoje Simic was involved in bringing the paramilitaries there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my previous knowledge, I did not really interfere with the work of the Crisis Staff in any way. I did not express any interest in that. I was personally present when Stevan Todorovic telephoned from the command of the 17th Tactical Group, when he made this telephone call to Belgrade. He called Colonel Jeremic. I never heard Blagoje Simic call anyone. Whether he knew or not is something that I could only make assumptions about. Blagoje Simic seldom came to the command of the 17th Tactical Group. Stevan Todorovic was at the command much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's continue on this, because we're talking about information that was applied by Simo Zaric during his statement, and that's information on page 74. But let's continue on this. Simo Zaric was your assistant, or you were his supervisor and he was your assistant, if you want to call it, in Bosanski Samac. He reported to you.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was his job to find out what was happening in Bosanski Samac and report that to you, as the intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his task, and he informed me, he reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he reported to you with intelligence information of what was happening politically, what was happening criminally, what was happening militarily, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And being in Bosanski Samac, in the town, he was in a position to know what was happening, where you were a distance away?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He knew these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have no reason to disbelieve Simo Zaric's statement that Todorovic and Dr. Blagoje Simic brought those paramilitaries into Samac, or into Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have no reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness has already answered this question, and he said that he did not know about Mr. Blagoje Simic knowing about the arrival of the special units. He said that Stevan Todorovic was there and that he knew about this. And now the Prosecutor is leading the witness, trying to make him say something else, but he has already given a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, the question by the Prosecutor has taken a different turn, and it's proper, so the witness should be able to answer. So your objection is not sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, his objection to your statement was overruled, so could you repeat your answer again to my question. You have no reason to disbelieve Simo Zaric's statement that Stevan Todorovic and Blagoje Simic were involved in bringing those paramilitaries into Batkusa; you have no reason to disbelieve that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on with the arrival of the paramilitaries. You indicated that Colonel Nikolic had gone out, or you had talked to Colonel Nikolic about the situation, and that he had scheduled a meeting for the next day, for April 12th. Isn't that correct? That a meeting was agreed to for April 12th?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was agreed that the meeting would be held in Donji Zabar on the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you -- and then Colonel Nikolic had told you that representatives of the civilian authorities from Bosanski Samac would be present; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said, and upon his return he did say that they had been present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So upon his return, Colonel Nikolic's return, you spoke with him and he said "they," referring to civilian authorities, had been present; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he told you, sir, that Blagoje Simic was present at that meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic returned from that meeting, he said not only to me, but to the other members of the command as well, he told us briefly about what this meeting was about and what was said there, and he said that the representatives of the civilian authorities had been there. I think he actually enumerated the members who had been there, who had been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he told you, when he enumerated on those persons, that Blagoje Simic had been there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he also mentioned Blagoje Simic, that he mentioned Milan Simic as well. Then this Simeon. I don't know these people. I know he mentioned Stevan Todorovic too. So the representatives of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And also, in addition to the civilian authorities from Samac - and you mentioned Milan Simic, the defendant Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, and a Simeon - in addition to those representatives from Samac were Crni, Lugar, and Debeli, at that meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic said, that they were also at that meeting and that they showed him their official IDs, that they were members of the MUP of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were aware at that time that Blagoje Simic was not only a Crisis Staff president, but Blagoje Simic was also the SDS party president?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that he was president of the SDS in the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the defendant Blagoje Simic's presence with the Serbian paramilitaries on that day, isn't that consistent with Simo Zaric's statement that we just discussed previously, that Blagoje Simic was involved in bringing the paramilitaries to Batkusa? Isn't that consistent with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Prosecutor is leading the witness and making him guess whether the presence -- whether one's presence at such a meeting can have a certain significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vukovic. There is no -- your objection is misconceived, I think. The Prosecution will go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The objection was overruled, so you can answer the question. The question, again, is: Blagoje Simic's presence at that meeting with the paramilitaries, isn't that consistent with Simo Zaric's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that Blagoje Simic was involved or participated in bringing the paramilitaries to the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that in that context Simo Zaric made this statement. This meeting was also attended by the representative from Pelagicevo as well. I know that. Also from the civilian authorities. I did not know whether he had taken part in bringing these volunteers in either. Commander Nikolic asked for a meeting with these civilian authorities, and they responded to that invitation. He enumerated the people who were there at that meeting, and he said to us what had been agreed upon at the meeting, that these volunteers would be under the command of the civilian authorities, not under the military, because they were not within the then Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us continue, sir. Simo Zaric, in that document at page 64 and 65, talks about the establishing, prior to the war, of a shadow government, or a parallel government, by the Serbs in the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo. Were you aware of that? Were you receiving reports that that was happening?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that this shadow government, or parallel government, was called the Serbian Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo Under Formation?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that that is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you further aware, sir, that Stevan Todorovic had been named the chief of police of the Serbian municipality by this shadow government?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had this information. And I also had the information that Mico Ivanovic had been appointed commander of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think now would be a time to break and we could continue on with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simeunovic, before we broke, we were talking about the shadow government that had been established by the Serbs prior to the war, and you had indicated that a Serb municipality had been established, that Todorovic had been named chief of police, that Mico Ivanovic had been appointed commander of the Territorial Defence, or TO. Sir, were you also aware that a Crisis Staff had been established by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you further aware that Blagoje Simic, the defendant, was named president of the Municipal Assembly and then the Crisis Staff president?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had that information. I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you further aware that government bodies were being established in this shadow or parallel government, including an Executive Council, various positions were being filled? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you further aware that Stevan Todorovic was forming a police unit? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out about that when the group came, a group of 23 young people was sent, young men who were being sent for training. That's when I found out about the police, established by Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you further aware that Stevan Todorovic was ordered by the Municipal Assembly or the Crisis Staff, still prior to the war, to establish this police unit and coordinate it with the military and civilian authorities, including the TO? Were you aware of that too?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly someone had to give him orders, and it was the Crisis Staff. They probably ordered him to set up this unit, but they had no cooperation with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir: Were you aware that the SDS municipal board initiated the appointment of Blagoje Simic as assembly president and then Crisis Staff head?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was appointed to these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So basically, prior to the war, there were several SDS or Serb activities involved in forming a government, this shadow government or parallel government?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with this question, but actually, it contains two questions. SDS or Serb activities. This makes a difference. I mean, SDS is a political party and Serb as ethnic group. This is not the same thing, at least for the Defence. Maybe the Prosecution has a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. I think it's better to split it and be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so prior to the war, there were several SDS and Serb leadership activities, or other Serb political party joint activities in forming a government, this shadow government or parallel government?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I assume that you being a Yugoslav didn't support these separate actions of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was in favour of Yugoslavia. I was a Yugoslav by conviction. I wanted things to stay the way they were. After that point, I wanted to continue that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you aware that the national Serb government leader, or former leader, an SDS party leader, national SDS party leader, Biljana Plavsic, has pled guilty in this court and has been sentenced just last week in this courthouse? Are you aware of that, sir? And she was sentenced for persecution of the non-Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as part of her plea, she has admitted to several things, and I'd like to read something to you and ask you how consistent that is with the information we were just discussing. On page 3 of the factual basis for her plea, paragraph 12 -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have this in B/C/S, and it's one paragraph. It might be easier if I read it and the witness followed along in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that part of the record, this paragraph you're trying to read? What is the formal document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this point, I'd ask that it be given an ID number. It's the factual basis for her plea of guilty. It's part of the record in that plea, and it's mentioned in the sentencing judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd invite your attention to paragraph number 12 on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to read that to you, and would you follow along with it. Paragraph 12: "In addition, the SDS prepared and distributed written instructions to SDS municipal leaders to form crisis staffs, proclaim Serbian municipal assemblies, and carry out preparations for the formation of municipal government bodies, and to mobilise Bosnian Serb police and Territorial Defence forces and subordinate them to JNA command. The municipal crisis staffs implemented these objectives and directives in the field, including ultimately the objective of ethnic separation by force." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we still don't see it on the ELMO. I really tried here on the screen, on the video evidence, it is not visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness is following as the Prosecutor was reading, and it is now on record. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, those orders which Biljana Plavsic indicated that the SDS leadership sent out to the municipal crisis staffs to take certain actions, those actions were all followed in Samac. That's what happened in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I get an ID number on that? I have the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D169/3 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it also says here to place them under the command of the JNA in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, the forces that had been set up were not put under the command of the JNA. It was only later, when Djordjevic, Crni, was named as commander, that they did join in, but at that point they joined the army of Republika Srpska. These forces were not under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get that to in a second. Let's work on the administrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we have one problem here. The number for this document is D169/3. This would mean that it's a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, can we go back to this document where you are quoting? It's a Prosecution Exhibit. It shouldn't be given an ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to just straighten that matter out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution Exhibit. It's an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this point, yes, it's a Prosecution document. I'd like it ID'd, the English and the ter version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What I'm saying is it's part of the record of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of that case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then I would move that it be admitted in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P164, and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to your last question, the Crisis Staff and, actually, the Municipal Assembly, Serbian Municipal Assembly, indicated that this police unit and the military units were to collaborate with the civilian and military authorities. However, based on your statement, they did not actually follow through and do that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police forces that were set up, they were not under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I can understand that. They were supposed to collaborate and work together, subordinate themselves with the JNA, but apparently in Samac they did not do that; they didn't follow through and do that; they didn't work together with the JNA. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not cooperate with the JNA in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, this document, it was filed under seal. Has it been lifted? Has the confidentiality been lifted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it was, in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you still have Exhibit P142 ter in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that still with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Simo Zaric also discusses the basis of these pre-war activities by the SDS, and these pre-war preparations for establishing a shadow government, and he discusses that in his June 3rd, 1998, interview, on page 65 of 142 ter. Now, if you go down to the fourth sentence, the name John, to the left, is asking a question. The question, page 65: "It didn't replace the government that was already in existence, but could have been called a shadow government, if you will." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 56 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. 65, sir. Do you see the name John, the fourth name down, with a question?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Simo Zaric is asked the following question: "It didn't replace --" And they're referring to this shadow or parallel government set up by the Serbs. "It didn't replace the government that was already in existence, but could have been called a shadow government, if you will." And the answer is, if you -- there's then the interpretation in -- okay. I just read it in English. Then there's the interpretation of question that, then there's the statement in B/C/S and then under that the statement in English again. And I'll read it in English if you would follow in B/C/S: "You could put it that way, yes, but it was all dictated by the Main Board, which was headed by Mr. Karadzic, and Blagoje Simic, who was the president of the Crisis Staff in Samac and took over the power, was a very close associate in agreement with Mr. Karadzic. I can say this because I found this out later, after the war had started, because I could see in which direction they were preparing themselves, and this is my conviction, and this is my opinion which I based on that." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric's statement that the municipal leaders were given orders by the national leaders, like Karadzic and Plavsic, that's consistent with the statement that Biljana Plavsic gave, where we gave the following orders to these people. Isn't that consistent, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We [as interpreted] certainly received instructions from our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one second. The answer that the witness gave was not: "We certainly received instructions from our superiors." It was: "They received instructions from their superiors." This is exactly what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can just have the answer repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat your answer to whether or not Zaric's statement was consistent with Plavsic's statement as to the establishment of the shadow government, as the orders coming down from the top? You said that they received instructions from their superiors. Is that how you answered that question of mine?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The municipal ones that were established, they certainly received instructions from their superiors, from the SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer to another one of Simo Zaric's interviews, P141 ter, please. Pages 11 and 12, please. Sir, what I'd like to do is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, you could sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What I'd like to do, sir, is move on from the shadow government into the takeover, and Simo Zaric, at pages 11 and 12 in that statement that was given to the Office of the Prosecutor, discusses Blagoje Simic's role in the takeover. And if you look at the bottom of page 11, where it says "Nancy" on the left, right at the bottom, the question was: Did you ever find out whether Blagoje Simic played any role in giving the orders for the attack to take place?" Zaric, top of page 12: "I already told you that Nikolic told us that it was President Blagoje Simic of the Crisis Staff had called him and told him that the Crisis Staff had decided that they would take over the town. So, yes, I do believe that he played a key role in the takeover." And if we go down to the next two paragraphs down, where you see "Nancy" again, or actually, four, she says: "I'm sorry. I may have missed this along the way. When was it that Nikolic received this call from Simic, informing him that they had made the decision to take over?" And Zaric responds: "And Nikolic told us that he had received a call from Blagoje Simic on the 16th, after midnight, so it was actually the 17th, very, very early in the morning, in the night, telling him that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town of Samac and that it would then become the Serbian municipality of Samac, that there were Serbian police and units were taking over all vital buildings and objects in the town." Did I just read correctly what Simo Zaric said? Did I just translate that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you've read this out correctly. It does make sense, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The translation basically is similar, but it is not word to word same as it is in the interview. So maybe it would be helpful to put it on the ELMO so the interpreters could have it before their eyes. Or maybe rather, the witness can read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO machine and read it from there, please, sir. And could you please read the phrase or the sentence that you indicate that is not correct, the interpretation is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several such sentences. What I said is that the general meaning is what you said, but the text itself is not exactly consistent with your reading. But the meaning is there. And still, there are several sentences which have a slightly different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you read those sentences out so we could put it in the record. Could you read it, that question and how Zaric responded.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where should I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 11, the first -- the question asked by Nancy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Prosecution counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 11, that last question. Begin with that. Nancy: "Did you ever find out whether Blagoje Simic played a role?"

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It starts --

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Did you ever find out whether Blagoje Simic played any role in giving the order for the attack on the town?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you read the answer on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I told you that Mr. Nikolic, the commander, that morning told us that the president of the Crisis Staff, Blagoje Simic, had informed him that they had taken the decision to take the town. This means - I'm talking about the Crisis Staff and I'm talking about Blagoje Simic. Therefore, I believe that Mr. Simic was one of the key people in bringing such a decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
