utterances.text: Okay. And then there's some requests for some water and then there's another question by Nancy: "I'm sorry. I may have missed this along the way." Do you see that? When was it that Nikolic received this call from Simic?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read that again, please.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on this page. There's only the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see the question and the answer? Does it follow, the question and the answer, sir? It's in the middle of page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May I point it out to the witness, walk over, to save time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the question, but the answer is not on the same page; it's on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please read the question and answer, up to the discussion -- the end of the police taking over the vital buildings, because there's other discussion there too.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is: "Excuse me. I may have missed this. When was it that Nikolic -- when was it that Blagoje Simic called Nikolic to tell him about the decision?" The answer is: "Mr. Nikolic told us that he had been informed on the 16th, after midnight, by the Crisis Staff, that the Crisis Staff had taken over power in the town, and so on and so forth. That means that was on the 17th, in the morning, or thereabouts. I don't know exactly. But at any rate, Mr. Simic informed him during the night that the Serb police forces and volunteers had come in to take the vital buildings and facilities and that they were taking over as the Serbian municipality of Samac. "If I may just be allowed to say this: This official government, Mr. Simic and the official government, during the war years, whenever they celebrated that day, the 16th, they considered it as the liberation day, you know. Personally, I don't share this opinion, but they always emphasised the role played by the Serbian police and volunteers, but never the 4th Detachment, never. They never wanted to mention that. What I want to say is: We really didn't - and this is not about pride - what I'm saying is that this is their entire strategy. They're making history anew. But I don't think history will be written in that way. For them, we were always a unit of traitors."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the statements that Zaric gave in this interview, are those consistent with your memory of what Nikolic said on that evening, or in those early morning hours, about receiving the telephone call from Blagoje Simic that the Serbs had taken over with the police and the paramilitaries? Is that consistent with your memory of Nikolic's statement during those early-morning hours?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know of any reason why Colonel Nikolic would have said that to Radovan Antic, to Simo Zaric, to yourself, if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the truth. That is what he said to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is leading the witness to speculate, purely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vukovic. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is not sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified last Wednesday and Friday about the transfer of the prisoners to Brcko. Do you recall that, testifying last week about that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And based on the information that you were receiving, you also talked about what was happening there in the town to the prisoners and civilians, that some bad things were happening in that town at that same period, which even resulted in prisoners being transferred.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The prisoners were removed for humanitarian reasons, in order to protect them. That is why they were transferred to Brcko. That was the primary reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified about the mistreatment of prisoners upon arrest, including extortion being -- they were being extorted upon arrest, and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the information that we received. That is the information we received when the commander ordered Simo to go to the police station to look at the statements that were taken from individuals who had been arrested and, if necessary, to conduct some interviews. He then noticed that these people had been mistreated, beaten up, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you received information, in addition to mistreatment upon arrest, mistreatment while in detention; mistreatment was taking place in the detention?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that in the detention, there were cruel and inhumane conditions, beatings and tortures, and you even saw prisoners all black and blue when you removed them. So the cruel and inhumane conditions in that detention?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you further had heard that one or more prisoners had even been killed, been murdered?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was exactly on that date, the 26th of April, when this decision was passed, that the killing had actually taken place, that the murder had taken place, and that is why the decision was passed to have them transferred to Brcko immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, you, as a professional military officer, wanted no part of any of this mistreatment upon arrest, mistreatment of prisoners, cruel and inhumane conditions, killing of prisoners. You, as a professional soldier, wanted no part of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't want to be any part of that. I opposed that, even when I came to Brcko, when the military policemen were also receiving these prisoners in a very rough manner. I opposed that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, did you also learn sometime during that time period, or sometime thereafter, that certain prisoners were being unlawfully arrested? You talked about Commander Nikolic having to call to have those JNA soldiers released, that certain people were being unlawfully arrested.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After authority was taken over, it was the members of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army who were also detained, and Commander Nikolic intervened with Stevan Todorovic and sent Simo Zaric in order to have these people released, and indeed they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, these five types of mistreatment or criminal acts that I just described above - mistreatment of prisoners upon arrest, mistreatment of prisoners in detention, cruel and inhumane conditions in detention, prisoners, one or more prisoners being killed, unlawful arrests - those five criminal acts, are you aware that Biljana Plavsic has pled guilty to the crime of persecutions, indicating that she and members of the Bosnian Serb forces, Bosnian Serb political and government organs and their agents, committed five of those acts that I just read to you? Were you aware of that, that among the crimes of persecution, or among the factors of persecution, were those five acts? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that Biljana Plavsic confessed her guilt. Perhaps the reporting was not very detailed in our part of the world, but they did say that Biljana Plavsic had confessed to her guilt and that that is why this judgement was passed upon her.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: She has admitted and been sentenced for persecution of the non-Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what she pled guilty to, admitting those five different types of acts, were the same thing that was happening in Samac, because you've just admitted that those things were happening in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there had been detentions in Bosanski Samac, and also inhumane treatment of the non-Serb population. They were detained in Serb [as interpreted] Samac. That was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And she admitted that she was involved in a campaign to commit those types of acts, and that amounts to persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The witness didn't say "Serb Samac," as it is here in the transcript on page 50, line 2. He said "in Bosanski Samac," is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: And she admitted that she was involved in a campaign to commit those types of acts, from the leaders on down, and those acts amount to persecution; do you agree with that? When you commit those types of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. [Interpretation] The witness is not a legal expert, and he cannot define persecution. It's better for the Prosecutor to ask the witness first what he means by "persecution," and only then he can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, Your Honour. That sounds good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic has pled guilty and has been sentenced for persecution against the non-Serb population of Bosnia, which you know, and the acts which constituted persecution included those acts which we just discussed were occurring in Samac. So what Biljana pled guilty to, therefore, was the same thing that was happening in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are now talking about persecutions in Samac, I cannot claim that there were persecutions in Samac. I said that I took part in the commission for exchange. No one from the commission for exchange forced anyone to leave Samac, to leave Bosanski Samac, their houses, and to go somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the exchanges later. Right now the question is: Those acts, unlawful arrests, mistreatment of prisoners upon arrest, mistreatment of prisoners in the detention facilities, murder of prisoners, inhumane and cruel conditions in the detention facilities - those acts which you admit occurred in Samac, Biljana Plavsic has testified -- or actually, Biljana Plavsic has pled guilty to being involved in those exact same acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could give such information for this objection, because I'm ... My colleague Mr. Vukovic already said that the witness is not a legal expert, and furthermore, this is not just these acts. There is also some other elements of this crime. Putting it this way to the witness and asking him whether it is a crime of persecution or not, it's far beyond his knowledge, his legal knowledge and his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor put a question to the witness, a very leading question. He never said that there were illegal arrests. The witness never said so while he was making his own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has testified about those five things, those five crimes, including the unlawful arrests, because that's why we also mentioned -- specifically we mentioned that Colonel Nikolic had to call and have certain JNA or 4th Detachment members released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. That was regarding the -- some members of the 4th Detachment. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the fact that Nikolic called and asked for some persons from the 4th Detachment to be released does not mean that they had been unlawfully arrested. That is what the Prosecutor says. That's not what the witness said. And the police cannot arrest the military, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Apparently they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But the point Mr. Vukovic is making that the fact that he ordered their release does not mean that they were unlawfully arrested. Because we haven't got evidence as to why or how they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit P127, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you go to paragraph beginning paragraph 5, or the fifth paragraph. It's on page 2 in the English. It should be 2 or 3. Do you see that paragraph, sir? It begins with: "The fact that criminals of a Yugoslav calibre were hiding among the Serbian commandos." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me read the fifth paragraph to you, the third sentence down, the third -- or the fourth sentence down, this is the 13th signatories document which was mentioned to you previously. You indicated you were aware of that document. Remember? Thirteen officers signed it, complaining of certain crimes that were being committed in Samac. If you read the fourth sentence down in that fifth paragraph, it says: "The massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims followed, without any criteria, and some prisoners were subjected to measures such as abuse, torture, and even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it indicates that persons were being arrested and isolated without any criteria.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you look at the last page, where the signatures are. Those are the signatures of the brigade command. Mile Beronja, Milan Josic, Simo Zaric, Jovan Erletic, Milan Maksimovic. Do you see those 13 names?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know of those persons?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know most of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know of any reason why they would be discussing arrests without any criteria if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wouldn't be any reason. There must have been a reason why they discussed this and why this kind of paper was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And also in that paper, they talk about mistreatment of prisoners, in addition to the isolation and arrests they mention in that same sentence that mistreatment of prisoners, including torture and even killing. Remember? They mentioned in that one sentence the mistreatment of prisoners too. Do you want me to read the sentence again to you? "The massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims followed, without any criteria, and some of the prisoners were subjected to measures such as abuse, torture, and even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin."

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony last week, I presented my own knowledge, that is, that detainees had been beaten up, and it is people like that, beaten up, black and blue, that I transferred to Brcko. And to the best of everyone's knowledge, they got these bruises while they were being arrested or upon arrest. The conditions were inhumane, their conditions of detention. And it is because of all of that that a decision was made to transfer them to Brcko, to the garrison in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these people who were being mistreated and were placed in inhumane conditions, these people that you then transferred to Brcko, these were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, sir. Let us talk about exchanges for a few moments. You testified this morning about your involvement in the exchange process; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that you were involved in the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the military commission for the exchange of prisoners of war and missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You weren't involved, sir, in the exchange of civilians. Your involvement was in the exchange of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in the exchange of prisoners of war, not civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And not being involved in the exchange of civilians, you didn't expect -- you didn't inspect any of the camps in Bosanski Samac after that one -- after the one transfer of prisoners to Brcko; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not visit these camps where civilians had been detained, except for the 26th, when I came to transfer those detainees to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of the condition of the prisoners in the primary school during the summer -- during the late spring and the summer and even early fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were detainees at the elementary school as well. This was later. This was not immediately at the beginning after the 17th. It was later. I know they were detained there, but I did not know under what kind of conditions they were. I had never gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after the movement of prisoners to Brcko, you never visited or examined the condition of the prisoners at the SUP or the TO, the civilian -- non-Serb civilians who were being held at the TO. You never examined their condition or met with them or visited them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is for cross-examination, but I think it would be fair to put the following question to the witness: Whether there were any detention in Samac after people were transferred to Batkovic. Because this line of questioning refers to Batkovic, but he does not ask whether there was anyone at the TO or the SUP after that particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm wondering whether the translation. Is Batkovic right there? I thought we were talking about Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I referred to, after the movement of prisoners to Brcko, that he basically had no -- I was trying to show he had no -- he had no visits or no opportunity to ever see those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I beg your pardon. My oversight. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: After the Brcko incident, which was the end of April -- on or about April 26th, April 28th, did you ever visit or see or meet with any of the prisoners at the SUP, the police station or the SUP, the TO or Territorial Defence, in Samac, during the spring, the summer, or fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not encounter these people after that. After the transfer, I did not come to the police station. I didn't go to the Territorial Defence building in Samac either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in addition to those other three facilities which we've mentioned - the primary school, the TO, the SUP - there were also non-Serb civilians that were held or isolated in Zasavica or at the high school, and you never visited or met with any of those people at those locations, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I know that there were people in Crkvina, let's say, in isolation, and also in Zasavica, a village. But I didn't visit, because there were no prisoners of war being held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you didn't visit these people in isolation because you -- they were civilians, these non-Serbs. They were civilians, and you were interested in the prisoners of war, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was only interested in prisoners of war. I was a member of the commission. I was not interested in civilians. I mean, they interested me as people, but I was not in charge of their release or their exchange. I simply didn't have that sort of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And since you weren't involved with the civilians, you never conducted any study or review of the voluntariness of the exchange of these civilians from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not conduct any studies, but I know that when we did go to exchanges, and when exchanges were agreed to be held in the Republic of Croatia, in Dragalic, or in the Gradacac area, or in the Doboj area, where people from Bosanski Samac did go, civilian people, I'd come the day before or the same day and I would go to the Red Cross. As far as I know, especially as concerns Brcko, the civilian population volunteered to appear at the Red Cross and apply for a possibility to be exchanged. They wanted people to secure a possibility for them to cross into the zone of responsibility of the HVO or the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, would you agree with me -- you were just mentioning that what you knew about Brcko, you were just talking about Brcko. But let's return to Samac for a few minutes. And was Simo Zaric in a position -- in a better position than you were to know what was happening in Samac in relation to the exchanges? Was Simo Zaric in a better position than yourself?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Simo Zaric was not involved with the commission for exchanges. Perhaps he was informed when an exchange would take place or when an exchange would not take place. Perhaps he knew even before I did. But I don't see that he was in any way involved in these exchanges, and he never appeared at the exchanges. I don't remember having seen him even at a single exchange where I was present in Samac. I don't remember Simo attending any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you: You were both intelligence officers in the past. Was Simo Zaric -- I'm not asking you yet about his involvement. My question is: Was Simo Zaric in a better position, being in Samac, than you were, who was outside of Samac, in knowing about those exchanges?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my colleague from the Prosecution must make this more specific as to which period exactly he is referring to. We know how long Mr. Zaric stayed on in intelligence jobs and when the exchanges took place. So if my friend wishes to continue with this line of questioning, if he could please specify the time period when Simo Zaric exactly was better informed on the exchanges, including Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll accept the suggestion of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1992, while you were outside of Samac and Simo Zaric was inside of Samac, obviously Simo Zaric was in a better position than you were to know about the exchanges and judge the exchanges; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly he knew perhaps more about that, simply because he was in Samac. But as to the working method of the commissions, that's something I don't think he knew about. I certainly know more about that than he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. What I'm talking about is the voluntariness of the civilians, of whether or not they were voluntarily leaving. He, being there, had a better opportunity to talk to the people, and had a better advantage than you had, because you weren't in Samac speaking to those people; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly he did have that advantage. He could have known or actually knew those people. He had more information as to whether those people were leaving of their own free will or whether they had been forced to leave. He certainly knew more about that than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P141 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you go to page 89, please. Turn to page 89. Could you look on the left, the second time, where it says "Nancy," where it's in the middle, where she asks a question. I'd like to read this to you, and you've indicated Simo Zaric was in a better position than you to judge the voluntariness of those people who were leaving. Nancy: "So it would be fair to say that they felt they had no choice but to leave Samac?" Answer, Zaric: "I think they had no choice. This is my opinion. It is the terrible truth, but it's the truth." Nancy: "Do you think that was true for most of the non-Serbs in Samac?" Answer: "Yes. That's my opinion. I think I have the right to my opinion. I saw that on the list there were many of my family members, relatives, neighbours, friends, over 200 people." Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason why Simo Zaric would say that those people had no choice in whether or not to leave or that they were not leaving voluntarily if it wasn't true? Do you know of any reason why Simo Zaric would say that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only give you my opinion on this why Simo may have said this, in view of the beatings we talked about, a certain insecurity that was in the air. A lack of certainty, precarious living conditions. It was easier to deal with situations where you found someone in the family, and that may have been the reason why people chose to go, why people wanted to go. I think that must be what Simo meant. But it's possible that he knew about pressure being exerted on certain individuals who then had to speak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take your answer in two parts. Let's start off with -- let's start off with the prisoners. We'll talk about prisoners, people in detention and people who were -- who are not in detention. First, with regard to those people in detention, you would agree that if a person is being held in inhumane conditions, as you described - beaten, tortured - we've had testimony that they had their teeth pulled in this case, that they faced death. You never know what day Lugar or the paramilitaries will come in and kill you. In that situation, if you're asked whether or not you want to leave Samac, you have no choice but to say "Yes, get me out of here." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have thanked them for making it possible for me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Simo Zaric's statement, you weren't there when he says that these people had no choice but to leave and he's referring to the non-Serbs, you weren't there to determine what force or pressure was placed on these people to leave. You weren't there to make that determination. Simo Zaric was in a much better position to make that determination than you, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I wasn't there. I was not in a position to determine that. Certainly Simo was better placed to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he indicated that those people had no choice, in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue on with the exchanges. This morning you were shown a document, D166/3, which was the rules and regulations for the work of the commissions of exchange for prisoners of war. And remember, we were looking at Article 13, where it talked about one-for-one exchanges, soldier for soldier, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person. Do you recall that this morning?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that document didn't say male soldier for male soldier, correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that document didn't say that, but the document was from the command of the East Bosnian Corps and it was meant for military commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. But it didn't say male soldier for male soldier or female soldier for female soldier. It didn't say either of those things, did it?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it didn't say elderly soldier for elderly soldier?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It said elderly person for elderly person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. So what it had was basically two categories: Soldier for soldier, or a second category, if you want to call it, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I explained the rules, I said that the whole thing applies to conscripts, to military conscripts, and a woman could be a military conscript too. It didn't necessarily have to be a man. And elderly person too could be a conscript. It didn't necessarily have to be a young person. That's in the parenthesis. One thing is the principle, but then in the parenthesis, the commission abided by -- there were arrests. Let me give you an example. A man was in military reprimand in Tuzla. He's 72 years old, but his role is given as scout. He couldn't even -- he had poor eyesight. He couldn't even stand up properly. And still, he was classified as scout. So perhaps that was also why we had to detain elderly persons. There were a lot of elderly persons in the prisons. We could not have set an age limit of between 20 and 30 years and then find elderly people aged perhaps 60 or 70 years old there. That's why the regulation was there. Elderly person for elderly person. That didn't strictly mean that no one could cross, that no one would be allowed to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if they were all considered soldiers or conscripts, all you would have to say is soldier for soldier. There would be no need to say woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person. If they're all soldiers, there's no need for those additional categories. Isn't it true that those categories covered mixed situations or mixed exchanges, where you had both soldiers and civilians being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The rules were used by military commissions alone, and military commissions were not involved in civilian exchanges. I'll say this again why this applied: Because there were elderly people who either came to the units of their own free will or they were treated as prisoners of war. Whether a certain person really was a prisoner of war, we couldn't tell, but if the person came from the military remand prison in Tuzla, we accepted him as such. I am not saying that all people at Batkovic were prisoners of war, but they were all treated as prisoners of war. That was how I went about it as a member of the commission. These are prisoners of war and people coming from the military remand prison in Tuzla are prisoners of war, those on their side. And that's why we had this rule woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person. It had nothing to do with the civilian commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Batkovic, and regardless of whether these people were prisoners of war, they were all treated as such at Batkovic. Were you at Batkovic often in late 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there often, but I was there sometimes, because sometimes it was my duty to go there. We would go there to determine whether the people requested by the other side were in Batkovic. And later, when we would forward and deliver lists for the exchanges, we had to make sure that those persons were in Batkovic at that point in time, so that they could be transferred. That was the purpose why I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you at Batkovic in December of 1993, when Miroslav Tadic was there? I'm sorry. December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Batkovic together with him. I don't remember us ever being together in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So not being in Batkovic, you cannot really testify today as to Miroslav Tadic's actions or activities at Batkovic. You weren't there to observe them.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that moment, but I can testify about the procedure, about the principles governing the work there. In case a member of one of the civilian commissions came. As I said, a member of a civilian commission could go to Batkovic, but prior to that, they had to obtain consent or approval that they were merely taking over prisoners on the day of a scheduled exchange, and even that for purely technical reasons. So that someone from Banja Luka would not be made to go to Batkovic and all the way back, but they needed consent. Without any prior consent, they would not have been able to enter Batkovic or talk to anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you were involved with providing consent to him to go there, but you weren't there, obviously, to see his activities while he was in Batkovic. You weren't present for any of his actions. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the activities, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said, further, that you couldn't replace a name on a previously approved list. You provided that testimony this morning; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a list was approved, if consent was secured from the security organ of the corps, we could not change the list without again requesting approval from the security organ. They gave their consent as to who could leave Batkovic, and only those who were on the list, only those who had been approved, could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could consent be obtained by telephone in a last-minute situation?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, usually you would indicate that the rules wouldn't allow that; is that correct? The rules would not generally allow that; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The rules would not allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, sir, during the war, didn't a lot of things happen that violated the rules or were not done according to rules, such as the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac removing Colonel Djordjevic and appointing Crni as the commander of the brigade? A lot of things happened not according to the rules; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Many things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just want to be clear with the answer of the witness. Is he also agreeing that the Crisis Staff did remove Colonel Djordjevic and appoint Crni in his place, or is he just agreeing to the fact that many things did happen which were not according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that was really a two-part question that I asked. I'm sorry about that. You've agreed many things happened not according to the rules. Are you also confirming your testimony of Friday, that the Crisis Staff was involved, from what you knew from Colonel Djordjevic, the Crisis Staff was involved in his removal and in the appointment of Crni? Are you maintaining that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I maintain that he was removed by the Crisis Staff. That was what Colonel Djurdjevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Colonel Djordjevic [sic] was the one that was removed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurdjevic. Djurdjevic. Djordjevic was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mico Djurdjevic was removed. Am I pronouncing the name incorrectly? Mico.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Djurdjevic, Djurdjevic. Not Djordjevic. D-j-u.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was removed, and rather than say his last name, we'll use his nickname. Crni replaced him, was appointed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And all of this happened, based on what you learned, at the request or at the insistence of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found out about that upon return at the command post, when Colonel Djurdjevic told me about what had happened at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to one more quick topic before the break and then we'll do one topic after the break and be finished. I want to ask you some questions about the military, and you've been here and told us about your whole career in the military, and you've mentioned the use of a logistics unit inside of a military unit. Logistics is basically the supply unit, if you want to call it, for a military unit?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's the supply of everything, from weapons to ammunitions to uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's the supply of fuel, food, all sorts of equipment and the repair of that equipment?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is part of it, all the necessary things, not in terms of combat operations but necessary for the normal functioning of a unit. All that is considered logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say it's necessary, it's vital, because it all concerns the operation of the army or the unit. If people aren't being fed, if they don't have ammunition, if they don't have weapons, the army doesn't function, so it's vital to the functioning of that military unit that you have logistics?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the important features.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's not always a simple situation either to be in a logistics unit, because it's rather complex. It involves storage, supplies, dispersing the equipment, recordkeeping, and also planning for those unit's needs. You don't just hand things out; you have to plan what you're going to bring in to your supply and what you're going to disperse. It involves a lot of planning?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And for the unit to function, you have to be -- the logistics unit to function, you have to be aware of the military unit's plans. You don't know what sort of ammunition to supply if you don't know of the plans or operations of that unit. You don't know how much food to bring in and allocate if you don't know the plans. So you have to -- the person in logistics, in charge, has to know about the operations of the military unit so that he can properly -- he or she can properly plan.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to look at this separately. Logistics for the lower-ranking units and logistics for the higher-ranking units. Those in the lower-ranking units did not need to know about the plans drawn up by the higher commands. He only secured the equipment for his own unit, and he had no need to secure equipment for three or five days, say, unless he had been ordered to do so. They had what they had in stock. And if we talk about ammunition, that was one combat set. Those in the lower units had to know about that. They had to secure a combat set for each member. But they didn't have to know the plans of the higher units. They didn't need to plan ahead, a month or two. He just sent his own needs on to the higher unit, and that's all he needed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we break now and come back to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our 20-minute break and come back at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simeunovic. When we -- just before we broke, we were talking about the logistics unit, and you indicated there was a difference between the higher-level units and the lower-ranking units, the logistics, that the lower-ranking unit logistics don't have to know what the higher-level logistics -- or what the higher-level command's plans were. However, sir, isn't it true that at least the lower-ranking units would have to know their own plans so they could determine their own needs? The commander or assistant commander running that logistics unit would have to know what the unit is doing in order to determine its needs at that lower level.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When answering these questions, I'm answering questions about all the units of the army of Republika Srpska, and also of the JNA. I'm talking about the principle of work of all subordinated units, all the lower-ranking units for logistics, as well as the higher-level units. I'm speaking quite generally about the principles governing the work in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And even in the former army of the JNA, it was very similar. You had things happening at various levels: The command logistics and the lower-level-unit logistics?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was practically the way it was in the JNA. So perhaps I can put it that way, that that's the way the army of Republika Srpska operated, according to the same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the jobs of -- or the responsibility of logistics would be -- could be extensive, or it really was extensive. For example, in Samac, the kitchen which was set up through the logistics unit, the kitchen fed not only the JNA soldiers and the 4th Detachment soldiers inside of Samac, but were you aware it also fed the paramilitaries too?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which period we're talking about now when this kitchen was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In April, right after the takeover of Samac. If you know. You might not know. You might not have been aware of it that the kitchen was established and was feeding everyone, including the paramilitaries. Did you receive that information in intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That kitchen that had already been established, that is to say, by the 17th it was supposed to have been established, or rather, before that there was no kitchen, because military conscripts were at their homes. They were not staying at military barracks or under such conditions. Part of the 4th Detachment, members of the 4th Detachment, after the 17th, was living under barracks conditions, if I can put it that way, and for them there was a kitchen. But this kitchen did not provide for the volunteers and the rest. They were fed at the village of Obudovac. They were staying there after their arrival, and that's where they got their meals. The military --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, sir, after the takeover, when the paramilitaries were mainly in Samac, at the different detention facilities or camps, they had to eat, and that kitchen, according to Mr. Tadic's testimony, was feeding those paramilitaries. Maybe you weren't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I object. [Interpretation] This is a total misinterpretation of Mr. Tadic's testimony. Mr. Tadic said that there had been two kitchens, that he organised the kitchen in Tekstilac, that that is the one that was for soldiers and that in that kitchen, members of the special unit did not receive their meals there. It was in the other kitchen. If the Prosecutor is referring to Mr. Tadic's statements, then the Prosecutor should read it properly and quote it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Tadic organised kitchens and that paramilitaries were being fed from one of them?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a kitchen was organised attached to the command of the 4th Detachment, and that is only where the members of the 4th Detachment only were being fed, nobody else. As for this other kitchen, I don't know who organised it or where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you -- did you ever eat at that kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were never at the door examining those persons who were entering and exiting the kitchen before and after meals?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that obligation to check who was entering and exiting. I entered the command of the detachment, and that is where only members of the command of the detachment entered, or rather, not only the command; members of the command and also members of the entire 4th Detachment, those that needed to come to the command. While I came to the command of the 4th Detachment, I did not see volunteers ever coming there. I never saw any such thing. But I did have knowledge -- I told you about that - that they had walked up once, and when they mistreated Radovan Antic, commander of the detachment. But I did not see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Last question: You talked about various levels of units, higher units, lower-level units. Was the 4th Detachment a lower-level unit? Is that how you were describing various levels of units previously.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was a unit which was within the 17th Tactical Group but that could exist independently as well. It was at battalion level. It had the rank of a battalion. But units in the army of Republika Srpska and in the army of Yugoslavia, it is only battalion units that can exist independently. Companies, no. They have to be subordinated to a higher-level unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Let's move on to another subject. Yesterday you were questioned about the - I'm sorry - on Friday you were questioned about the relationship or the lack of relationship between the SDS and the JNA. Do you recall that? You were questioned by Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, there were questions, but I don't know which specific question you're referring to now. Perhaps you could remind me. I know that there was something that had to do with that, but I don't know which question you are exactly referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you weren't aware of any relationship between the JNA and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not work on some common objectives, if I can put it that way, that is to say the SDS and the JNA. We, as the Yugoslav People's Army, had interests that were contrary to the objectives and interests of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, earlier you were shown a statement, the factual basis of a plea by Biljana Plavsic. Remember we were looking at that, looking at that earlier? That's P164. Remember you were looking at that earlier. And you were aware or you are aware that Biljana Plavsic at one point was the highest-ranking SDS official in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that she held a high office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you also know that she has admitted to collaboration between the SDS and the JNA? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what I read, if I understood this correctly, she admitted to her guilt, and also that municipal staffs were established and that everybody should be put under the command of the JNA. I said that in Samac, these forces that had been established were not put under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army, because the Yugoslav People's Army only handled units that belonged to it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P164. The question is about Biljana Plavsic right now and whether or not you're aware of her involvement in collaboration at the high level between JNA leaders and SDS leaders, and her statement is about that, and I'd like to show you two of them. 164 ter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 11. Let us look at paragraph 11, please. "In October 1991 and the months following, the SDS intensified efforts to ensure that the objective of ethnic separation by force would be achieved in the event that a negotiated solution did not occur. These steps included arming large segments of the Bosnian Serb population, in collaboration with, among others, the JNA, the Ministry of Interior affairs, MUP of Serbia, and Serbian paramilitaries, establishing Serbian military and police formations and coordinating with the JNA and paramilitary units from within and outside BH." Further, could you look at paragraph 19 on page 4 and read along with me, or I'll read it to you and you can follow along, please: "The Bosnian Serb military, police and civilian forces and authorities, under the direction and control of the SDS and the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the collective Presidency and the expanded collective Presidency, collaborated with the JNA, the ministry of internal affairs, MUP of Serbia, and paramilitary units from within and outside BH to implement the objective of ethnic separation by force. The Bosnian Serb military, police, and civilian forces, collaborating with the JNA, the MUP of Serbia, and paramilitary units, committed persecutions upon the non-Serb populations through a persecutory campaign." What I've read so far, in both of those statements, Biljana Plavsic talks about collaboration between the SDS and the JNA. Do you agree with that, what I just read? Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read it correctly, but let me just say one thing. In relation to Samac, in Samac there was the 4th Detachment, which was multi-ethnic. It did not include Serbs only. It involved Croats and Muslims too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, for the B and H, this is what Biljana Plavsic said. I cannot talk about her interests or her ideas or what she knew. But as far as the territory that I hail from is concerned, this is what the situation was, and that is what I'm describing to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you never attended any meetings with any of the national SDS leaders and the military, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to make -- I don't have a problem with this line of questions, but SDS and military, does that mean both together?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings between the SDS leaders, including Karadzic, Krajisnik, Plavsic, and the JNA leaders? Did you ever attend any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never appeared during any conversations of any of those persons, the JNA leaders and Krajisnik, Plavsic, Karadzic? You weren't present during any telephone conversations involving those persons?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Nor were you ever present for any conversations between Slobodan Milosevic and any of those SDS leaders relating to the JNA -- relating to plans for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never at any such place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you really can't report what plans were being made at the highest level between the Serb leaders, the Serb and SDS leaders from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Serbia, and the JNA; you really can't comment on those?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended such meetings, and I cannot speak about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on a little bit. And you talk about the evening or the early-morning hours of the takeover, where Blagoje Simic calls and indicates that the paramilitaries, at the request of the Crisis Staff, have taken over Samac. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were awakened by the person on duty, this is what Commander Nikolic said to us, that Blagoje Simic called him and that the Crisis Staff had taken over, that volunteers were at these vital facilities, and that the Crisis Staff had taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew at that point that Blagoje Simic was not only the Crisis Staff president, but he was also president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that before too, that he was president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that a Serb government had been installed and the legitimate government had been removed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think this witness is not a legal expert. Maybe the issue could be rephrased, because that's up to the Trial Chamber to determine whether certain government is legitimate or not. Because Defence has completely opposite position. Maybe the question should be framed in terms of multi-ethnic local government elected in 1990, and then to ask with regard to that. Because whether it's legitimate or not, it's a big question, in light of the facts that Defence is of the position that after the broke-up, after the failure of the Bosnian parliament in October 1991, there is no legitimate state and there is no legitimate system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the position of Defence. And maybe this witness can be confused with this line of questions. Legitimate or non-legitimate. It's a legal issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll use the word "elected government."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Or simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Instead of classifying it in any manner, simply use the word "previous government."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, he -- this witness has testified that the elected government had been removed from his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So I'll use -- I was hoping to use his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, you've testified that the elected government had been removed and a Serb government had been installed through the paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said - and if necessary, I can repeat it once again - the staff told us, Commander Nikolic told us, that the Crisis Staff had taken over, that it took power. I did not use any other word but "takeover." Takeover in cooperation with these volunteers. They took these vital facilities, et cetera. The Crisis Staff of the municipality of Serb Samac -- of the Serb municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So as a summary, the town has been taken over, the elected government has been overthrown, there is a new Serb government that's been installed, the Serb Crisis Staff is in control. And after knowing these things, Colonel Nikolic contacts his command and asks them what to do. Should he send the troops in, should we retake the town? He calls them and asks them for direction, and they basically tell him: Do nothing. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, when he got this information from Blagoje Simic, Commander Nikolic called the Superior Command, conveyed to them what had happened in Samac. The order given was to raise the level of combat readiness in all units of the 17th Tactical Group, but that nothing should be done, that the army should not be used. That moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They told you that the army should not be used. They didn't tell you to go in and reinstate the elected government; isn't that correct? They didn't tell you that, to go in and reinstate the elected government?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no such order. And we acted in accordance with the order that we did receive, raising the level of combat readiness. The army was not there to establish a government or to remove a government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The army was there to maintain the status quo, and the status quo had been an elected government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. I believe that the witness as a factual witness has very clearly explained what were the objectives of the JNA at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing that he said that would say that it was the status quo that was the topic of the army to keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't the JNA's duty to defend the constitution of Yugoslavia and to maintain the status quo?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the role of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is to say, to prevent the spread of war. That was the basic task that we had. The spillover of war from Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of the basic tasks of our unit at that time was that, in that territory. I already explained why there was this objective possibility of a spillover of the war. We proved this because we knew that the army of the Republic of Croatia was already interfering and was already issuing orders in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our task was to prevent the spillover to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the command was worried about a potential spillover. They were not worried about a group of paramilitaries and a Serb Crisis Staff taking over a town and removing the elected government; isn't that true? They weren't worried about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it's not quite the way you've put it. The army, the Yugoslav People's Army, cared about that too, and the transfer of people when killings occurred, a killing at the police station, the Yugoslav People's Army reached a decision to transfer these people to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, the Yugoslav People's Army did not say: Go in and retake the town and place -- or reinstall the elected government of Samac. They never said that. They never said: There's killings now, there's beatings, illegal arrests. You're to go in and reinstall the illegally-elected government. They did not do that; isn't that correct? The command never gave you that order.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command never gave such an order, but immediately after the takeover - I testified about that earlier - we had the knowledge that there were units that had already been established and that had been attached to that government, units that were paramilitary units, that already had its areas of responsibility, its commanders, et cetera. So we would be legalising these existing units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you don't do anything and go in and stop the situation, you are legalising those units and you're ensuring the survival of that Serb government which just took over and removed the elected government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the mass arrests and mistreatments started, the Yugoslav People's Army did not interfere. It was a matter for the politicians to resolve, to resolve that situation. However, when the physical liquidation of people started, that is when the Yugoslav People's Army interfered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, what you did was removed people from the SUP and the TO when there was a murder and beatings. You never went in and removed that government that police chief, you never reinstated or reinstalled the elected government, and that's because those were the orders you had received from the command; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did not receive such orders, and we did not act in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Instead, what you had done on that first day, on the 17th, you activated the 4th Detachment and sent them to the river banks to protect against any attack from either Croatia or any armed Muslim civilians, or whatever you want to call them. That's what you did.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the Yugoslav People's Army went to the border, if I can put it that way, to protect the border. This was on the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So since the commander, the Yugoslav's army, didn't have you do anything to prevent the takeover or to change the status of the takeover, but instead had you send in troops to prevent anyone from reinstituting the elected government or reinstalling the elected government, the only explanation is that the Yugoslavian army command agreed with what was happening or that they were working with the paramilitaries or collaborating with the paramilitaries; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a very long question, so I'll have to -- first of all, I believe it should be divided. First of all, it's calling for speculation. What would, for example, a Croatian side do if they come back to Samac? Would they reinstall a government that was elected in 1991 or not? That's the first question. The witness couldn't know that. No one could answer to that question. And furthermore, the consequences that my colleague is talking about, that they actually agreed with what happened and things like that, this is -- I don't believe that this witness is the one who can answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. First of all, it's loaded, and part of the speculation is actually true. Nobody would have known if the Croatian army had got into the area in question, what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the fact that the command told you to do nothing, basically, told you not to interfere, isn't that consistent with Biljana Plavsic's statement that the JNA was collaborating with the SDS and the Serb political leaders, and that's why they didn't want anything done there?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That's not what it's like. Biljana Plavsic said that all those units should be placed under the command of the JNA, but they were not placed under the command of the JNA. Therefore, even after the events, after the 17th, this group was not under the command of the JNA until Djordjevic, Crni, was appointed as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was distanced from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is: The fact that the JNA command did nothing, isn't that consistent with Biljana Plavsic's statements that the SDS and the Serb political forces were collaborating with the JNA? Isn't that consistent? At the highest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he can answer that question. First, my colleague really asked him very carefully, this witness, about whether he was present on such negotiation of such meetings, and now he asks him to speculate about if there was any such agreement at the highest level of JNA and SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. The question is clear. He's simply asking whether that situation was not consistent with what Biljana Plavsic has said in her statement in admitting her guilt. He's merely asking that part, whether or not that was consistent.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If at that moment the JNA, when the takeover happened in Bosanski Samac, did not take any measures, it didn't necessarily mean that the JNA was in agreement with the situation that was there. We, as the Yugoslav command of the JNA, still had the same view that we had had on the 15th or on the 12th of April, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir, the fact that the JNA never took any action to remove the Serb government that was put in by the Crisis Staff and the paramilitaries and reinstate the elected government, that they never took any action, isn't that consistent with Biljana Plavsic's testimony -- or statement, not testimony - that the JNA and the SDS and the Serb political leaders had all collaborated at the highest levels? Isn't that consistent, sir?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. If the JNA decided to interfere in every single municipality where there had been a takeover, then what would the JNA be? It would be some sort of a policeman patrolling the area. Its purpose was not to preserve the government of a given municipality. Its purpose was to prevent the war from spreading into the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, please move on. I think we've been on this point for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Last matter on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with General Veljko Kadijevic? He used to be the Yugoslav federal secretary of Defence. Are you familiar with who he is?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that he has written in his auto biography that after the disintegration of Yugoslavia, that the JNA -- sorry, that the JNA concentrated upon the protection and the defence of those ethnic Serbs who, in the course of the disintegration, found themselves outside of Serbian Montenegro? Were you aware of that, that that's what he felt, the general, thought that's what their responsibility was, the protection of the Serbs? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So once again, assuming that is true, my statement, what I've just made to you, the fact that the JNA command told you to do nothing and that the JNA didn't do anything, isn't that consistent with the statements of Veljko Kadijevic and the statements of Biljana Plavsic, a collaboration between the Serbs and the JNA at the highest levels?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll say this again. In our area of responsibility, in the area of responsibility of the 17th Tactical Group, there were mixed units of the JNA, and that runs counter to what Biljana said. Perhaps she was talking about a more general level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the command decision not to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm in no position here to discuss what it was like in the top command ranks of the JNA, because I was only a member of the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you can't answer for -- answer or really indicate what their policies were at that time at the high levels, at the highest levels. You can't answer what their policies were. You're not aware of what they were.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I can't answer that. I don't know what their strategy was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our agreement is to start in this order. I only have several brief questions related to the cross-examination, relating to the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been shown one section of the interview given by Mr. Zaric. You explained prior to that to the Trial Chamber that your information concerning the exchanges was far greater in comparison to Mr. Zaric's information, given the amount of work you've done related to the exchanges. In the examination-in-chief, you said that Mr. Zaric worked on security affairs until April 1992 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the spring and summer of 1992, there were three exchanges with the opposite side that took place in Samac and that one of those exchanges was actually organised by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that those exchanges took place, but I was not present when they took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't think I appreciate what you are saying, that our agreement is to start in this order. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant is that I should start the re-direct, because my questions were related to the exchanges. I'm not sure if Mr. Pantelic has any other questions. We did not exactly decide at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The procedure is that the counsel calling the witness re-examines at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but you made it possible for us in our additional examination, should any issues be raised during the cross-examination that are related to the other two defences, that first the other two Defences should have the right to ask the first questions, and then finally the party calling the witness. It was in that sense that I was saying I meant to ask the first questions, because they're directly related to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So do you know that representatives of the International Red Cross at any given point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was no discussion during the Prosecution's cross-examination relating to the International Red Cross or the local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give up this line of questioning, but the questions asked by Mr. Weiner related to Mr. Zaric's information and knowledge related to the spring and summer of 1992, and that was demonstrated by the interview given by Mr. Zaric about the exchanges in which the International Red Cross took part too. But as the witness just stated that he had no direct knowledge of that, I'll just drop this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the period that you worked on the exchanges with civilian commissions, mostly, and what I really want to know about is the Samac commission, did you ever notice that any civilian or prisoner would go to an exchange against their own free will? Did you ever notice a prisoner or a prisoner about to be exchanged who did not want to be exchanged and yet was made to go to an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps my explanation was not detailed enough. I did not wish to go into the technical details of the exchanges themselves. But when an exchange is organised and once you reach the separation line, the opposite side asks the persons who arrive from our side whether they wish to be exchanged or not. They had to say it loud and clear, in front of them. And there was never a single case that anyone came up and said: I was forced to come to this exchange. There were cases where people refused to be exchanged, and then those people would return to their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not what I wanted to ask you, because we've heard enough about that before this Court, such testimonies. In a position where, for example, a person from Batkovic was being taken for an exchange and decided not to be exchanged, would they return to Batkovic or would they go to their own home?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was no discussion of that during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Not in cross-examination. About where they would return to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just be allowed to say --
