utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was shown a section of an interview by Mr. Simo Zaric concerning the element of free will as involved in the exchanges, and this question of mine arises directly from the Prosecution question posed to the witness about the free will and Mr. Zaric's interview when prisoners were taken to an exchange. Part of a person's free will is the possibility to refuse to be exchanged and to go back home. I think this is directly related to questions asked by the Prosecution when showing the witness the interview by Mr. Zaric, and they did want the witness to give his own opinion on why Mr. Zaric said some of the things, so I must get this clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. I think the relationship is so close to the question that you had posed. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we again have this document, this interview, shown to the witness, the last section of the interview by Mr. Zaric. He said this is only my own opinion and I am entitled to my opinion. Now, the question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Persons from Batkovic who were approved for an exchange, who went to an exchange, and then they would say there loud and clear whether they wanted to be exchanged or not, and the Trial Chamber knows this, so in case they refused to cross to the other side, would they go back to their own homes or would they be returned to detention? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a person would have been free to go and would not be returned to detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The opposite side, during negotiations and talks, representatives of the other side, did they ever tell you that any of the people who had been exchanged had ever told them that they had been forced to be exchanged? Did you ever learn anything like that from the other side in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commissions that we were in negotiations with never told us anything like that. They never told us: Well, why did you bring those people the last time around by force? They never told us anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I'd just like to ask the witness -- it's just a question following up from Mr. Lukic. And Mr. Lukic had asked you, concerning persons from Batkovic, whether -- if they refused to cross, whether they could go back to their own homes or they would be returned to detention. And you said they would have been free to go and would not be returned to detention. And I'm just interested to find out how you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that because of a case in Brcko, where a man said that he did not wish to be exchanged, and he did not wish to go to leave for a third country through the International Red Cross, but rather wanted to return to Brcko, and then he was subsequently returned to Brcko. Not a single person was returned to the collection centre from an exchange taking place. Either there was a third exchange, but mostly people wanted to cross to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simeunovic. My learned friend and colleague Mr. Weiner from the Prosecution asked you about whether Mr. Blagoje Simic had any role in bringing in the volunteers from Serbia. You will remember that, won't you? You specified that there was Stiv Todorovic and so on and so forth, and then the Prosecution read out sections of the interview given by Mr. Simo Zaric to the Prosecution, where Mr. Simo Zaric claims that it was his view that Blagoje Simic too had been involved in that. You remember the Prosecutor asking you that?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think my colleague Mr. Pisarevic, last week, asked you, in terms of your position in the 17th Tactical Group, you had daily reports coming in from the commander for security at detachment level. You'd collect these reports and analyse them. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was the usual modus operandi?

utterances.speaker: MAKSIM SIMEUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were regular, daily reports that were delivered every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm merely repeating what you said, because I'm trying to lead you to a different subject that I wish to broach now. On page 11, that's Simo Zaric's interview dated 2nd of April, 1998, and page 12, the question by Ms. Nancy Paterson, the Prosecutor, was, addressed to Simo Zaric -- I'm reading this to you now. I want you to analyse what you hear: "Did you ever find out -- Ms. Paterson says that Blagoje Simic had played any role in giving the order for the attack on the town. And then Simo Zaric - I'll omit the first part of his answer - says that he believes that Mr. Simic was one of the key people in taking such a decision. So you have Mr. Zaric's precise wording. He believes. And then if you compare that to what you've been read out by the Prosecution with what seemed a hundred per cent certainty. But I should assume that Mr. Zaric himself was not really positive about these developments and how exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That question is unintelligible. It's multiple questions and it's more of a speech too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's very precise. I will rephrase. It's no problem. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simeunovic, can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will continue the next time we are able to continue with the witness, because other proceedings are waiting for the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may address very briefly to the Trial Chamber. It is about Mr. Mirko Pavic who gave his 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have received on Friday late afternoon the English translation of his interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have already given this statement to the Prosecution, and I have here enough copies for the Trial Chamber. So if it is appropriate moment, I believe we should deal with this promptly. Maybe it is a moment to offer this for evidence, this statement of Mr. Mirko Pavic so the Trial Chamber can look at it and maybe issue some decision after hearing what the Prosecution would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can have it numbered for identification purposes only, and have the Prosecution indicate -- no, no, no. This is the witness -- this is the witness who is a heart patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the witness who is -- yes. No, no. Well, actually, he had a brain stroke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The one I had suggested that because he has this problem, why can't he have his statement and then he can just appear for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make an exception in this case because of his health. So we don't have to ask the Prosecution to indicate. They will go ahead and cross-examine. Because we have this limited period for videolink, so we'll just have to make that exception. Yes. But we'll still have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D43/4, and ter. That's "D" as in David.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow with videolink. The witness will continue, because we haven't finished with you, Mr. Simeunovic. We'll continue -- your counsel will be able to indicate when we will be through with the videolink witnesses. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, I've just been informed that my colleague didn't raise that issue. With regard to the line-up of witnesses for videolink, first witness will be Grujicic, Mr. Grujicic. Second witness is Savo Popovic. And the third witness is Pistoljevic. Due to the fact, Your Honour, that I was just informed yesterday from Mr. Savo Popovic, he is a high-rank official in the spot or position of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the Republican level, Muslim Croat level and Republika Srpska, very serious conference which should be in Bijeljina on Friday, at noon. So with that regard, we moved him prior to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he will be the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He will be the second one, yes. Thank you for your understanding, and I do apologise to my friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
